# Probability Distributions {.hero #s04-distributions}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="4"}
Seminar 4 · Binomial, Poisson, exponential, normal
:::

## Random Variables {.formula-slide #random-variables}

::: {.lede-min}
A random variable is not really a variable. It is a rule that hands every outcome in the sample space a number, which is what lets us do arithmetic with chance.
:::

$$X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \qquad\qquad P(X = x)$$

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.fragment}
[Discrete]{.col-head}
[Values you can list]{.col-sub}

Roll two dice and let $\color{#93C54B}{X}$ be the total. It is the number already written in every cell of the board.

```{=html}
<div class="perm-row"><span>3 + 4</span><span>2 + 5</span><span>6 + 1</span></div>
```

Six of the thirty-six cells carry a 7, so

$P(\color{#93C54B}{X} = 7) = \tfrac{6}{36}$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Continuous]{.col-head}
[Values filling a range]{.col-sub}

Wait at a bus stop and let $\color{#325D88}{X}$ be the minutes until the next arrival. It can be 3, or 3.1, or 3.0004.

```{=html}
<div class="perm-row"><span>3.0</span><span>3.1</span><span>3.0004</span></div>
```

No single value can carry any probability, so ask for a stretch instead

$P(2 \le \color{#325D88}{X} \le 4)$
:::
::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
Which kind you have decides the tool. A discrete variable gives every value its own probability and you add them up. A continuous one spreads probability along a line and you measure the area under a curve. The binomial and the Poisson ahead are discrete, the exponential and the normal are continuous.
:::


## A Distribution Is a Function {.formula-slide #distribution-fn}

::: {.lede-min}
Hand $P$ a value of $X$ and it hands back the probability of that value. That function is the distribution, and writing it down once replaces all the counting.
:::

$$\sum_{k} P(X = k) = 1 \qquad\qquad \int p(x)\,dx = 1$$

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.fragment}
[Flip a coin four times]{.col-head}
[$\Omega$ has sixteen outcomes, $\color{#93C54B}{X}$ counts the heads]{.col-sub}

```{=html}
<svg width="338" height="186" viewBox="0 0 338 186" aria-label="probability of each number of heads in four flips"><rect x="22" y="119" width="46" height="17" rx="3" fill="#93C54B"/><text x="45" y="110" font-size="15" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">1/16</text><text x="45" y="159" font-size="16" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#3E3F3A" text-anchor="middle">0</text><rect x="84" y="67" width="46" height="69" rx="3" fill="#93C54B"/><text x="107" y="58" font-size="15" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">4/16</text><text x="107" y="159" font-size="16" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#3E3F3A" text-anchor="middle">1</text><rect x="146" y="32" width="46" height="104" rx="3" fill="#93C54B"/><text x="169" y="23" font-size="15" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">6/16</text><text x="169" y="159" font-size="16" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#3E3F3A" text-anchor="middle">2</text><rect x="208" y="67" width="46" height="69" rx="3" fill="#93C54B"/><text x="231" y="58" font-size="15" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">4/16</text><text x="231" y="159" font-size="16" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#3E3F3A" text-anchor="middle">3</text><rect x="270" y="119" width="46" height="17" rx="3" fill="#93C54B"/><text x="293" y="110" font-size="15" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">1/16</text><text x="293" y="159" font-size="16" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="#3E3F3A" text-anchor="middle">4</text><line x1="8" y1="136" x2="330" y2="136" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="169" y="178" font-size="15" font-family="Roboto, sans-serif" fill="#6E7681" text-anchor="middle">number of heads</text></svg>
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Why bother]{.col-head}
[Three things the function buys you]{.col-sub}

**One summary.** Write $P(\color{#93C54B}{X})$ once and every probability is already in it, with no sample space left to count.

**A model.** The distribution is a claim about the process, so data can test it and estimate the numbers inside it.

**Arithmetic.** Add the bars over a range, or measure the area under the curve, and you have $P(a \le \color{#93C54B}{X} \le b)$.
:::
::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
The two examples ahead already have names. Heads in $n$ flips is the **binomial**, and a height or a measurement error is the **normal**, written $\color{#93C54B}{X} \sim \text{Binomial}$ and $\color{#325D88}{X} \sim \text{Normal}$.
:::

## Laplace's Rule of Succession {.stage-slide #laplace-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
In 1774 Laplace said not to rate a seller $k/n$. Credit one imaginary good review and one bad one, then rate them $(k+1)/(n+2)$.

## Where the Binomial Comes From {.stage-slide #binom-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Every review is an independent draw at one constant unknown rate $S$. We cannot work back to it, only forwards. Suppose $S$ and see what it predicts.
:::

## What If the Rate Were Different? {.ojs-slide #likelihood-live}

::: {.lede-min}
One guess at $S$ gives one number. Turn the dial and the top plot reshapes, while the bottom traces that number against every $S$ it could be.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof s = Inputs.range([0.50, 1.00], {value: 0.95, step: 0.01, label: "True success rate s"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
n = 50
k = 48

// The deck's palette, so the plots match the hand-drawn stages either side.
PAL = ({olive: "#93C54B", brick: "#B94A48", navy: "#325D88",
        orange: "#F47C3C", soft: "#6E7681", dim: "#B0B7C0"})

// Binomial pmf by recurrence: P(0) = (1-p)^n, then
// P(j) = P(j-1) * (n-j+1)/j * p/(1-p). No factorial is ever formed, so
// nothing overflows — the same route stage-kit.html uses.
pmf = function (p) {
  const q = 1 - p;
  if (q <= 0) return Array.from({length: n + 1}, (_, i) => (i === n ? 1 : 0));
  let v = Math.pow(q, n);
  const out = [v];
  for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) { v = v * ((n - j + 1) / j) * (p / q); out.push(v); }
  return out;
}

pk = pmf(s)
value = pk[k]
lik = d3.range(0, 1.0005, 0.004).map(sv => ({s: sv, p: pmf(sv)[k]}))

PSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  // marginTop 16, not 4: at 4 the 30% tick label has no room above the top
  // gridline and reads as cut off. Height grows to match so the plotting
  // area is unchanged.
  width: 950, height: 154, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
  style: PSTYLE,
  x: {domain: [-0.6, n + 0.6], ticks: d3.range(0, n + 1, 5), label: null, tickSize: 4},
  // labelAnchor centre rotates the label down the axis; Plot's default puts
  // it at the top, where it sits on the top tick.
  // Both plots are pinned to 0-30% so the two heights read against the same
  // scale. This one does exceed it once s passes about 0.97 — at s = 1 every
  // draw is fifty ticks, so that bar is 100% — hence clip, which flattens it
  // at the top of the frame instead of letting it paint over the equation.
  y: {domain: [0, 0.30], ticks: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], grid: true,
      tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d), label: "P(k | s)",
      labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(d3.range(n + 1), {x: d => d, y2: d => pk[d], strokeWidth: 5,
      stroke: d => (d === k ? PAL.olive : PAL.dim), clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ojs-eq">P(<span class="hit">48&#10003;</span>, <span class="miss">2&#10007;</span> | s = <span class="rate">${s.toFixed(2)}</span>) = <b>${value.toFixed(4)}</b></div>`
```

```{ojs}

  // marginTop 16, not 4: at 4 the 30% tick label has no room above the top
  // gridline and reads as cut off. Height grows to match so the plotting

  width: 950, height: 154, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
```

## The Binomial in Standard Notation {.formula-slide #binom-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
Everything so far, in the notation the worksheet uses. The rate we have been calling $S$ is written $\color{#F47C3C}{p}$; its complement is $\color{#B94A48}{q} = 1 - \color{#F47C3C}{p}$.
:::

$$P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \binom{n}{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\; \color{#F47C3C}{p}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}\; \color{#B94A48}{q}^{\,\color{#B94A48}{n-k}} \qquad X \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n, \color{#F47C3C}{p})$$

::: {.fragment .note}
One review is a **Bernoulli trial**, a single attempt with two outcomes, scored $1$ for good and $0$ for bad.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$P(B_i = 1) = \color{#F47C3C}{p}, \quad P(B_i = 0) = \color{#B94A48}{q}, \quad \operatorname{E}[B_i] = \color{#F47C3C}{p}, \quad \operatorname{Var}(B_i) = \color{#F47C3C}{p}\color{#B94A48}{q}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$X \;=\; B_1 + B_2 + \cdots + B_n, \qquad B_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\color{#F47C3C}{p})$$
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Each of seller B's fifty reviews was one $B_i$. The binomial is nothing more than their sum, which is why only the count survives.
:::

## The Rare Event Limit of a Binomial Distribution {.ojs-slide #pois-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Hold the average $\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} = n\,\color{#F47C3C}{p}$ still and push $n$ up. Each trial gets rarer, but you expect the same number of events.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof nTrials = Inputs.range([10, 400], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Trials n"})
// Floor of 10, not 5: lam runs to 8, and n < lam would ask for p > 1, which
// the recurrence below happily turns into a 1971% gap. NB a comment must NOT
// be the first line of an {ojs} cell: it shadows the '//|' directive and
// Quarto then emits the whole slide as plain source, with no runtime and no
// error anywhere.
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lam = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 3, step: 0.5, label: "Mean λ = np"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
PPAL = ({olive: "#93C54B", brick: "#B94A48", navy: "#325D88",
         orange: "#F47C3C", soft: "#6E7681", dim: "#B0B7C0"})

pp = lam / nTrials                       // the success rate, shrinking as nTrials grows
KMAX = Math.max(12, Math.ceil(lam + 4 * Math.sqrt(lam)))
ks = d3.range(0, KMAX + 1)

// Binomial(nTrials, pp) by the same recurrence used everywhere else in this deck
binom = {
  const q = 1 - pp;
  if (q <= 0) return ks.map(k => (k === nTrials ? 1 : 0));
  let v = Math.pow(q, nTrials);
  const out = [v];
  const top = Math.min(nTrials, KMAX);   // KMAX <= 20; no point walking to 20,000
  for (let j = 1; j <= top; j++) { v = v * ((nTrials - j + 1) / j) * (pp / q); out.push(v); }
  return ks.map(k => (k <= nTrials ? out[k] : 0));
}

// Poisson(lam): P(0) = e^-lam, then P(k) = P(k-1) * lam / k
pois = {
  const out = []; let v = Math.exp(-lam);
  for (let k = 0; k <= KMAX; k++) { out.push(v); v = v * lam / (k + 1); }
  return out;
}

gap = d3.max(ks, k => Math.abs(binom[k] - pois[k]))
YMAX = Math.max(d3.max(binom), d3.max(pois)) * 1.18
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 205, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 26, marginTop: 16,
  style: {fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
          color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [-0.6, KMAX + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YMAX], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ks, {x: d => d, y2: d => binom[d], strokeWidth: 9,
      stroke: PPAL.dim, clip: true}),
    // "step" is Plot's midpoint step (d3.curveStep); "step-mid" is not a
    // curve name and throws, taking the whole plot cell with it.
    Plot.line(ks, {x: d => d, y: d => pois[d], stroke: PPAL.brick,
      strokeWidth: 2, curve: "step", clip: true}),
    Plot.dot(ks, {x: d => d, y: d => pois[d], fill: PPAL.brick, r: 3.2,
      clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ojs-eq">Binomial(${nTrials}, <span class="rate">${pp.toFixed(4)}</span>) &nbsp;→&nbsp; <span class="miss">Poisson(${lam.toFixed(1)})</span> &nbsp;·&nbsp; gap <b>${(100*gap).toFixed(2)}%</b></div>`
```

::: {.slide-footer}
Watch what is lost. Push $n$ up and the shape stops revealing $n$ or $\color{#F47C3C}{p}$, only their product. That is why the Poisson has *one* parameter.
:::

## The Poisson in Standard Notation {.formula-slide #pois-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
Put $\color{#F47C3C}{p} = \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}/n$ into the binomial and let $n$ run away.
:::

$$P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \binom{n}{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\big(\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{\color{#93C54B}{k}}\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{n-\color{#93C54B}{k}}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Group the factors by whether they still mention $n$]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$=\;\frac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}}{\color{#93C54B}{k}!}\;\cdot\;\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-\color{#93C54B}{k}+1)}{n^{\color{#93C54B}{k}}}\;\cdot\;\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{n}\;\cdot\;\big(1-\tfrac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}{n}\big)^{-\color{#93C54B}{k}}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [As $n \to \infty$ those three go to $1$, to $e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}$, and to $1$]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$P(X = \color{#93C54B}{k}) \;=\; \frac{\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}^{\,\color{#93C54B}{k}}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}}}{\color{#93C54B}{k}!} \qquad X \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda})$$

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Only the middle factor did any real work, since $(1-\lambda/n)^{n}$ *is* the definition of $e^{-\lambda}$. One parameter now does the job of two, and $\operatorname{E}[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}$.
:::

## Check the approximation {.sim-slide #pois-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · exact vs approximate
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Three mistakes per 10,000 transactions; 10,000 audited. What is the chance of four or more? Compute it both ways.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
n <- 10000
p <- 0.0003   # <-- keep n * p = 3

binomial <- 1 - pbinom(3, n, p)
poisson <- 1 - ppois(3, n * p)

c(binomial, poisson)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Both read `0.3527681`, so every digit R prints agrees and the approximation costs you nothing here. Now set `n <- 20; p <- 0.15` (still $np = 3$) and watch it open up. **That** is what "large $n$, small $p$" is protecting you from.
:::

## Time Between Poisson Events {.ojs-slide #expo-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Count arrivals, or time the wait. The bridge is the $\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}$ bar.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lamE = Inputs.range([0.5, 4], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "Rate λ per minute"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof winT = Inputs.range([0.1, 2.5], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Window t minutes"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
muE = lamE * winT                     // arrivals expected in the window
KMAXE = Math.max(8, Math.ceil(muE + 4 * Math.sqrt(muE)))
ksE = d3.range(0, KMAXE + 1)

// Poisson(muE) by the deck's usual recurrence: P(0) = e^-mu, P(k) = P(k-1) mu/k
poisE = {
  const out = []; let v = Math.exp(-muE);
  for (let k = 0; k <= KMAXE; k++) { out.push(v); v = v * muE / (k + 1); }
  return out;
}

// The whole point of the slide: the k = 0 bar IS the exponential's survival
// curve. P(no arrival in [0, t]) = e^(-lambda t) = P(wait > t).
p0E = Math.exp(-muE)
TE = 3                                // minutes on the bottom axis
densE = t => lamE * Math.exp(-lamE * t)
gridE = d3.range(0, 241).map(i => TE * i / 240)
tailE = d3.range(0, 161).map(i => winT + (TE - winT) * i / 160)
YPOIS = d3.max(poisE) * 1.18
YDENS = lamE * 1.12
ESTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 154, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
  style: ESTYLE,
  x: {domain: [-0.6, KMAXE + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YPOIS], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k arrivals in t)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ksE, {x: d => d, y2: d => poisE[d], strokeWidth: 7,
      stroke: d => (d === 0 ? PPAL.olive : PPAL.dim), clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ojs-eq">P(<span class="hit">0 arrivals</span> in ${winT.toFixed(2)} min) &nbsp;=&nbsp; <b>${p0E.toFixed(4)}</b> &nbsp;=&nbsp; P(<span class="hit">wait &gt; ${winT.toFixed(2)}</span>) &nbsp;·&nbsp; <span class="rate">λ = ${lamE.toFixed(1)}</span></div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 154, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 24, marginTop: 16,
  style: ESTYLE,
  x: {domain: [0, TE], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YDENS], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".1f")(d),
      label: "density of the wait", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    // This olive area is the same number as the olive bar above it.
    Plot.areaY(tailE, {x: t => t, y: densE, fill: PPAL.olive,
      fillOpacity: 0.3, clip: true}),
    Plot.line(gridE, {x: t => t, y: densE, stroke: PPAL.brick,
      strokeWidth: 2.5, clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([winT], {stroke: PPAL.soft, strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

## The Exponential in Standard Notation {.formula-slide #expo-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
The wait beats $t$ exactly when nothing arrives in $[0, t]$, so read the Poisson at $\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}$.
:::

$$P(T > t) \;=\; P\big(N(t) = \color{#93C54B}{0}\big), \qquad N(t) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t)$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Put $\color{#93C54B}{k = 0}$ into the Poisson formula]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$=\;\frac{(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t)^{\color{#93C54B}{0}}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}}{\color{#93C54B}{0}!} \;=\; e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [That is the survival curve, so the density is the slope of $1 - e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t}$]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$f(t) \;=\; \color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}\, e^{-\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} t} \qquad T \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda})$$

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
The same $\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}$, read the other way round. $\operatorname{E}[T] = 1/\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda}$ is the average gap between arrivals.
:::

Each one answers exactly one question.
:::

::: {.qcard .qcard-binom .fragment}
[$\operatorname{Binomial}(n, p)$]{.qcard-name} [How many successes in a fixed number of attempts?]{.qcard-q}
:::

::: {.qcard .qcard-pois .fragment}
[$\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$]{.qcard-name} [How many events happen in a fixed amount of time?]{.qcard-q}
:::

::: {.qcard .qcard-expo .fragment}
[$\operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda)$]{.qcard-name} [How long until the next event?]{.qcard-q}
:::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
The first two count and the third measures, so only the third has no $n$ and no $k$ in it.
:::


-->
## The Limit of a Binomial Distribution for Large n {.ojs-slide #normal-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Hold $\color{#F47C3C}{p}$ still and push $n$ up, and the bars settle onto a bell.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof nBig = Inputs.range([5, 200], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Trials n"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pBig = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {value: 0.35, step: 0.05, label: "Success rate p"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
muB = nBig * pBig
sdB = Math.sqrt(nBig * pBig * (1 - pBig))
kLo = Math.max(0, Math.floor(muB - 4 * sdB))
kHi = Math.min(nBig, Math.ceil(muB + 4 * sdB))
ksB = d3.range(kLo, kHi + 1)

// Binomial(nBig, pBig) by the deck's usual recurrence, walked only as far as
// the plot shows: P(0) = (1-p)^n, P(j) = P(j-1) (n-j+1)/j p/(1-p).
binomB = {
  const q = 1 - pBig;
  let v = Math.pow(q, nBig);
  const out = [v];
  for (let j = 1; j <= kHi; j++) { v = v * ((nBig - j + 1) / j) * (pBig / q); out.push(v); }
  return out;
}

// De Moivre's curve: N(np, np(1-p)), read as a density at each whole k.
normB = x => Math.exp(-((x - muB) ** 2) / (2 * sdB * sdB)) / (sdB * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))
gapB = d3.max(ksB, k => Math.abs(binomB[k] - normB(k)))
YMAXB = d3.max(ksB, k => Math.max(binomB[k], normB(k))) * 1.18
BWB = Math.max(1.5, Math.min(9, 880 / (kHi - kLo + 1) - 1))
gridB = d3.range(0, 241).map(i => kLo + (kHi - kLo) * i / 240)
BSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
           color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 950, height: 205, marginLeft: 64, marginBottom: 26, marginTop: 16,
  style: BSTYLE,
  x: {domain: [kLo - 0.6, kHi + 0.6], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  y: {domain: [0, YMAXB], grid: true, tickFormat: d => d3.format(".0%")(d),
      label: "P(k)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 56},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(ksB, {x: d => d, y2: d => binomB[d], strokeWidth: BWB,
      stroke: PPAL.dim, clip: true}),
    Plot.line(gridB, {x: d => d, y: normB, stroke: PPAL.navy,
      strokeWidth: 2.5, clip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ojs-eq">Binomial(${nBig}, <span class="rate">${pBig.toFixed(2)}</span>) &nbsp;→&nbsp; <span class="miss">N(${muB.toFixed(1)}, ${(sdB*sdB).toFixed(1)})</span> &nbsp;·&nbsp; gap <b>${(100*gapB).toFixed(2)}%</b></div>`
```

::: {.slide-footer}
Two limits come out of one distribution. Rare events with $\color{#F47C3C}{\lambda} = n\color{#F47C3C}{p}$ held still give the Poisson, plenty of events with $\color{#F47C3C}{p}$ held still give the normal.
:::

## Break the Bell on Purpose {.sim-slide #clt-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · the CLT, stress-tested
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-plot}
```{webr-r}
#| fig-width: 5.7
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
n <- 5             # <-- draws per average
pop <- function(k) rexp(k)^2   # no bell at all

xbar <- replicate(4000, mean(pop(n)))
hist(xbar, breaks = 40, col = "#CBD9E6",
     border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = paste("mean of", n, "draws"))

round(c(sd_obs  = sd(xbar),
        se_pred = sd(pop(1e5)) / sqrt(n)), 3)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
`n <- 1` is the raw population, violently skewed; by `n <- 30` it is nearly symmetric and `sd_obs` tracks $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. **The CLT is a claim about the mean, and it survives a parent this ugly.**
:::

-->

## The Normal Distribution {.ojs-slide #normal-formula}

::: {.lede-min}
That bell has a formula. $\color{#B94A48}{\mu}$ slides it, $\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}$ stretches it, and the area under it is always 1.
:::

$$f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}\sqrt{2\pi}}\; e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\color{#B94A48}{\mu}}{\color{#F47C3C}{\sigma}}\right)^{2}}$$

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// The density itself, on a FIXED vertical scale, so a small σ visibly
// buys its narrowness with height: the area never changes.
nfDens = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - nfMu) / nfSig) ** 2) / (nfSig * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))
nfGrid = d3.range(0, 401).map(i => -4 + 8 * i / 400)
nfPeak = nfDens(nfMu)
nfArrowY = Math.min(nfPeak + 0.1, 1.1)
// the reference N(0, 1), and the stretch within one σ of the centre
nfStd = x => Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)
nfBand = d3.range(0, 121).map(i => nfMu - nfSig + 2 * nfSig * i / 120)
NFSTYLE = ({fontSize: "15px", fontFamily: "Roboto, sans-serif",
            color: PPAL.soft, background: "transparent"})
```

:::: {.nf-row}
::: {.nf-left}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// The two dials, stacked in the left column; the plot takes the right.
viewof nf = Inputs.form({
  sig: Inputs.range([0.4, 2], {value: 0.84, step: 0.01, label: htl.html`Spread <b style="color:${PPAL.orange}">σ</b>`}),
  mu:  Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.34, step: 0.01, label: htl.html`Centre <b style="color:${PPAL.brick}">μ</b>`})
}, {template: ins => htl.html`<div class="nf-dials">${Object.values(ins)}</div>`})
nfSig = nf.sig
nfMu = nf.mu
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Three readings. Only the first moves: the area and the ±σ share are the
// same for every normal, which is the point of showing them beside it.
html`<div class="nf-card">
  <div><span>Peak height</span><b>${nfPeak.toFixed(3)}</b></div>
  <div><span>Area under the curve</span><b>1</b></div>
  <div><span>Within μ ± σ</span><b class="nf-band">68.3%</b></div>
</div>`
```
:::

::: {.nf-right}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 330, marginLeft: 56, marginBottom: 28, marginTop: 20, marginRight: 10,
  style: NFSTYLE,
  x: {domain: [-4, 4], label: null, tickSize: 4},
  // up to 1.1: room for σ = 0.4, whose peak is 0.997, and the arrows over it
  y: {domain: [0, 1.1], grid: true, ticks: [0, 0.5, 1], label: "f(x)",
      labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 46},
  marks: [
    // the reference: N(0, 1), dashed, behind everything
    Plot.line(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfStd, stroke: PPAL.dim, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5 5"}),
    Plot.areaY(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, fill: PPAL.navy, fillOpacity: 0.08}),
    // within one σ of the centre: always 68.3% of the area
    Plot.areaY(nfBand, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, fill: PPAL.orange, fillOpacity: 0.18}),
    Plot.line(nfGrid, {x: d => d, y: nfDens, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    // the peak, read across to the axis: 1/(σ√2π), never 1 unless σ ≈ 0.4
    Plot.ruleY([nfPeak], {x1: -4, x2: nfMu, stroke: PPAL.navy, strokeDasharray: "2 4", strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
    Plot.dot([nfMu], {x: d => d, y: nfPeak, r: 4.5, fill: PPAL.navy}),
    Plot.text([nfPeak], {x: -4, y: d => d, dx: 4, dy: -9, textAnchor: "start",
      text: d => d.toFixed(3), fill: PPAL.navy, fontSize: 14, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text(["N(0, 1)"], {x: 2.6, y: nfStd(2.6) + 0.07, text: d => d,
      fill: PPAL.soft, fontSize: 14}),
    Plot.ruleX([nfMu - nfSig, nfMu + nfSig], {y1: 0, y2: nfArrowY + 0.05,
      stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([nfMu], {y1: 0, y2: nfArrowY + 0.05, stroke: PPAL.brick, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.arrow([-1, 1], {x1: nfMu, x2: d => nfMu + d * nfSig, y1: nfArrowY, y2: nfArrowY,
      stroke: PPAL.orange, strokeWidth: 2.5, headLength: 10, inset: 4}),
    Plot.text([-1, 1], {x: d => nfMu + d * nfSig / 2, y: nfArrowY, dy: -12, text: () => "σ",
      fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text([nfMu], {x: d => d, y: nfArrowY + 0.05, dy: -12, text: () => "μ",
      fill: PPAL.brick, fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700}),
    // in the left half of the band, clear of the μ line at every σ
    Plot.text([nfMu - nfSig / 2], {x: d => d, y: nfPeak * 0.3, text: () => "68.3%",
      fill: PPAL.orange, fontSize: 16, fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: PPAL.dim})
  ]
})
```

<!-- commented out: moments-formal (merged into #moments)

## Mean and Spread in Standard Notation {.formula-slide #moments-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
The three pictures, written down. Each piece of a formula is a piece of the picture.
:::

$$\operatorname{E}[X] \;=\; \sum_x \underset{\color{#6E7681}{\text{where it sits}}}{x}\;\;\underset{\color{#6E7681}{\text{its weight}}}{\color{#325D88}{p(x)}} \;=\; \color{#B94A48}{2.24}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Replace each position by the area of its square, and average again]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$\operatorname{Var}(X) \;=\; \sum_x \underset{\color{#6E7681}{\text{area of its square}}}{\color{#F47C3C}{(x - \mu)^2}}\;\;\underset{\color{#6E7681}{\text{its weight}}}{\color{#325D88}{p(x)}} \;=\; \color{#F47C3C}{1.92}$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Read off the side of the average square, back in the units of $X$]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$\operatorname{SD}(X) \;=\; \underset{\color{#6E7681}{\text{side of the average square}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}} \;=\; \color{#325D88}{1.39}$$

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
For a normal these are exactly its two parameters: $\operatorname{E}[X] = \color{#B94A48}{\mu}$ and $\operatorname{SD}(X) = \color{#325D88}{\sigma}$.
:::

-->

## Unpacking the Normal Formula {.stage-slide #normal-build}

::: {.lede-min}
Every piece of the formula has a job. The $e$ and the square make the bell, $\sigma$ sets its width, $\mu$ moves it, and the constant in front keeps the area at 1.

::: {.note-box}
$Q_1$ and $Q_3$ sit at $\mp 0.6745\sigma$, so the fences fall at $\mp 2.698\sigma$ and only $0.7\%$ of a normal lies beyond them. In a sample of a thousand, about seven points get flagged with nothing wrong.
:::

Subtracting $\mu$ moves the curve; dividing by $\sigma$ squeezes it, so it grows *taller* — area is always 1. The shaded probability never moves: standardising changes the ruler, not the answer.

## Functions of a Random Variable {.formula-slide #funcrv}

::: {.lede-min}
For $\color{#93C54B}{Y} = g(X)$, work through the *CDF* and never the density. Ask which values of $X$ make $\color{#93C54B}{Y}$ small enough.
:::

$$F_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; P(a X + b \le y) \;=\; P\big(X \le \tfrac{y-b}{a}\big)$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [The right-hand side is just $X$'s own CDF, read at a shifted point]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$F_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; F_X\big(\tfrac{y-b}{a}\big)$$

::: {.deriv-arrow .fragment}
[↓]{.deriv-glyph} [Differentiate in $y$; the chain rule brings down the $1/a$]{.deriv-note}
:::

$$f_{\color{#93C54B}{Y}}(y) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{|a|}\, f_X\big(\tfrac{y-b}{a}\big) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \color{#93C54B}{Y} \sim \operatorname{N}\big(a\mu + b,\; a^{2}\sigma^{2}\big)$$

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Standardising is this with $a = 1/\sigma$ and $b = -\mu/\sigma$, which is why one table serves every normal. A *non-linear* $g$ leaves the family, so $X \sim \operatorname{N}(0,1)$ makes $\color{#93C54B}{Y} = X^{2}$ chi-squared.
:::

## The Chi-Square Distribution {.stage-slide #chisq}

::: {.lede-min}
Square $k$ independent standard normals and add them up. The total is never negative, and it is the yardstick for sample variances, since $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="chisq-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

## The Student's $t$ Distribution {.stage-slide #tdist}

::: {.lede-min}
Swap the unknown $\sigma$ for the sample's $s$ and the bell gets fatter tails. Formally $T = Z/\sqrt{V/k}$ with $V \sim \chi^2_k$, which is why the chi-square came first.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="tdist-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

## Relationships Among Probability Distributions {.formula-slide #dist-map}

::: {.lede-min}
Each distribution is one step from another: a sum, a limit, a square or a ratio.
:::
